name: Bicalutamide mesotherapy

card.summary: Scalp mesotherapy using the antiandrogen bicalutamide, discussed by people hoping to block androgen effects locally to slow hair loss.
card.note: Bicalutamide is an oral prescription drug; injected scalp use is not an approved route.

quick.overview:
Bicalutamide is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen that blocks the androgen receptor. Since androgens drive male-pattern hair loss, some hair-loss communities talk about delivering it to the scalp through mesotherapy (tiny injections or microneedling-assisted application) to act locally.
Bicalutamide is approved only as an oral tablet for prostate cancer. Its off-label oral uses in women include hirsutism, acne and scalp hair loss. No published trials of scalp mesotherapy exist.
quick.how: Discussion describes clinic or home mesotherapy with a bicalutamide preparation, usually compounded. No dosing or sourcing is given here. Users generally combine it in discussion with other hair-loss treatments.
quick.risks: Systemic bicalutamide causes breast tenderness and gynecomastia (up to 80% of men on monotherapy), hot flashes, reduced libido, erectile dysfunction and liver-test abnormalities; it is contraindicated in pregnancy. Whether scalp delivery reaches the bloodstream has not been studied.

lead: Bicalutamide (Casodex) is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen patented in 1982 and approved in 1995 as an oral tablet for prostate cancer; it blocks the androgen receptor without lowering androgen levels.[1] Wikipedia describes no topical or injectable formulation.[1]

Mesotherapy is the delivery of small amounts of a substance into the skin by injection. Combining it with bicalutamide is a practice discussed among hair-loss users hoping to counter androgen effects at the scalp while limiting side effects elsewhere.
Off-label oral use includes androgen-related skin and hair conditions in women, such as hirsutism, acne and scalp hair loss.[1]

angle.text: Proponents suggest a local antiandrogen could blunt the androgen signal behind pattern hair loss. This route is unapproved and unstudied.

paras: The drug is on the WHO Essential Medicines List and is sold as a generic in more than 80 countries.[1] Approved uses are metastatic and locally advanced prostate cancer; off-label uses include hirsutism, acne, seborrhea and scalp hair loss in women, feminizing therapy for transgender women and others.[1]

In men, breast tenderness and gynecomastia are most common, along with hot flashes, reduced body hair, low libido, erectile dysfunction and fatigue.[1] Liver test abnormalities occur and monitoring is recommended; rare interstitial pneumonitis and photosensitivity have been reported.[1] In women it can raise cholesterol and is contraindicated in pregnancy.[1]
